query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys under simultaneous wear and corrosion, the dominant mechanism governing degradation is a dynamic interplay between the mechanical rupture of a protective, passivating oxide film and its limited, localized repassivation. That is, sliding contact mechanically disrupts the passive film at asperity contacts faster than it can uniformly reform, thereby exposing fresh substrate to corrosion. This results in a synergistically accelerated degradation that is modulated by the alloy’s microstructural characteristics and alloying elements which influence the stability and repair kinetics of the oxide layer.
generation.material_initial_state: A well-processed, as-synthesized high-entropy alloy (e.g., an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi or similarly composed alloy) exhibiting a uniform, thin, passive oxide film formed by the natural affinity of its constituent elements (or via mild annealing) and displaying fine microstructural features.
generation.intervention: Perform controlled tribological sliding tests in a 3.5 wt% NaCl corrosive environment while systematically varying mechanical loads and sliding speeds. Parallel tests are conducted in an inert environment for comparison.
generation.conditions: Ambient temperature, with tests conducted using identical sliding parameters (load, speed, contact geometry) under two environmental conditions (one corrosive with NaCl and one inert via N2-purged atmosphere), ensuring electrochemical measurement of OCP and friction coefficient in real time.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity and dynamic behavior of the surface passive oxide film.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, mechanical shear and pressure locally rupture the protective passive film. Although the alloy’s inherent repassivation capability leads to partial film reformation, the damage is spatially and temporally nonuniform. This intermittent film rupture allows localized accelerated corrosion at fresh metal sites, and the repassivation kinetics—affected by microstructure and alloying additions—can’t fully compensate for the wear-induced losses, culminating in a synergistic increase in total degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to isolated wear in inert conditions or static corrosion tests, the tribo-corrosion tests will exhibit a higher overall degradation rate. In situ measurements will show characteristic fluctuations in OCP and friction that correlate with repeated film rupture and repassivation events. Moreover, alloys optimized with minor alloying additions (e.g., slight boron levels) that stabilize the passive film should exhibit lower combined degradation.
generation.baseline: Wear-only tests in an inert environment and corrosion-only tests under static conditions, both showing lower cumulative mass loss than the synergistic tribo-corrosion case.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under moderate mechanical loads and typical chloride concentrations (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl). However, at very high loads or in highly aggressive corrosive environments, the repassivation process may become negligible, limiting the applicability of the mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from PMC11378927 (which demonstrates dynamic passive film disruption under cavitation erosion–corrosion) and PMC10456374 (which shows how thermal treatment can stabilize passive films) supports aspects of this interplay, the exact kinetics of film rupture and repair under sliding conditions and the quantitative influence of microstructural features remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct parallel tribo-corrosion experiments on identical high-entropy alloy specimens under (a) a corrosive environment (3.5 wt% NaCl) and (b) an inert environment (e.g., N2-purged cell). Use a linear reciprocating tribometer equipped with in situ OCP and friction monitoring. After testing, perform detailed surface analysis (SEM/EDS) to assess passive film integrity.
measurements: Time-resolved OCP fluctuations indicating film rupture/repassivation events
Friction coefficient profiles corresponding to changes in interface strength
Wear volume and mass loss quantification
Surface oxide thickness and uniformity via SEM/EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tribo-corrosion tests in the corrosive environment do not show significantly higher degradation rates, or if there are no discernable fluctuations in OCP and friction that can be correlated to passive film rupture and repassivation (i.e., the results closely match the inert environment data), then the hypothesis that the dynamic rupture–repassivation of the passive oxide film governs the coupled degradation will be falsified.
